reader.title: Lynching of J. A. Archuleta
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A crowd of Mexicans took a prisoner accused of killing a deputy sheriff from jail and lynched him (A1, A3, A11).

A 'crowd of Mexicans' took the accused killer of Deputy Sheriff Blancett from jail and lynched him (A1, A13), and an army dispatch says a mob seized and lynched the 'Mexican murderer' before militia could arrive (A11); this meets the standard definition, but no paper describes the victim as Black.

The Denver Tribune's Santa Fe wire (A1, A3, A6) and an independent army dispatch to General McKenzie (A11) agree that the man who shot Deputy Blancett was lynched, though they differ on the place and on how he was held.

summary.text: The lynching of J. A. Archuleta took place on the night of Sunday, October 29, 1882, when a crowd of Mexicans took Archuleta, a justice of the peace and banker of Conejos, Colorado, from custody in northwestern New Mexico and lynched him.
He was accused of shooting and killing Deputy Sheriff Blancett a few days earlier.
Papers across the country carried the news chiefly because the dead man was a judge and 'prominent banker and merchant'.
According to a Santa Fe dispatch credited to the Denver Tribune, Archuleta shot and killed Deputy Sheriff Blancett at Farmington, New Mexico.
A separate dispatch from U.S. Army officers placed the shooting at Bloomfield and said that 'a Mexican' had wounded Eugene Blancett, who later died.
A German-language weekly added that Blancett was shot while trying to take the weapon from the enraged man.

Captain Haines, the local justice of the peace and militia captain, reported to the commander at Fort Canon Gallegos that he was 'powerless, as a mob wants to hang the Mexican', while about 150 armed Mexicans stood guard over the prisoner.
General McKenzie passed the report to Governor Sheldon, who ordered Colonel Max Frost to take a company of militia to Bloomfield to protect the prisoner.
Before Frost could start, word came that the prisoner had been 'taken from his friends and lynched' and that the mob had dispersed.
The wire version said that on Sunday night a crowd of Mexicans took Archuleta from jail and lynched him, and a Michigan digest said he was hanged.
No paper names the place where he was killed.
No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution of the lynchers appears in the coverage.
The German account suggested the lynchers may have feared that Archuleta's money would keep him from being convicted.

The Santa Fe wire ran nearly word for word from October 31 in papers from Washington and New York to Salt Lake City and Sacramento, with the names garbled as Archuletta, Archulatta, Arichuletta and Achuletia.
Headlines ranged from 'A Banker Lynched' and 'Lynching a Prominent Citizen' to the National Republican's 'Killed His Man and Got Lynched'.
Weekly papers in Texas, Ohio, Kansas and Michigan reprinted it into mid-November.

The Wheeling Register printed the army dispatch under the headline 'Too Late', and three weeks later its joke column remarked that a band played 'Nearer, My God, to Thee' as 'a Colorado murderer' was swung off: 'They do things in style out there.'
No paper in the coverage condemned the lynching.

The wire places the shooting at Farmington and says Archuleta was taken from jail, while the army dispatch places it at Bloomfield and says the unnamed Mexican was taken from armed friends guarding him.
The Crawford Avalanche put the jail at Conejos, 'New Mexico', which the wire gives only as Archuleta's Colorado home.

accounts.gist: Archuleta, a justice and banker of Conejos, Colorado, shot and killed Deputy Blancett at Farmington a few days earlier; on Sunday night a crowd of Mexicans took him from jail and lynched him.

accounts.label: Army dispatch via General McKenzie
accounts.gist: At Bloomfield 'a Mexican' shot Eugene Blancett; a mob wanted to hang him while about 150 armed Mexicans protected him; before militia could leave he was 'taken from his friends' and lynched.

accounts.label: German-language account
accounts.gist: Blancett tried to take the weapon from the enraged man, who shot him; the lynching is described as deliberate, possibly from fear that Archuleta's money would keep him from being convicted.

framing.detail: Most papers printed the Santa Fe wire verbatim under headlines such as 'A Banker Lynched' and 'Lynching a Prominent Citizen', stressing the victim's standing.
The National Republican's 'Killed His Man and Got Lynched' and the Kennebec Journal's 'A Murderer Lynched' presented the accusation as settled.
The Wheeling Register headed the army dispatch 'Too Late' and later joked that the lynchers hanged 'a Colorado murderer' to a band's hymn: 'They do things in style out there.'
